newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - RBA governor pushes for more labour reforms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - RBA governor pushes for more labour reforms.

text.p: Australia's central bank governor Ian Macfarlane strayed into politics on Thursday, challenging the government to undertake more labour market reform.
Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane told a Melbourne business lunch that reforms already carried out by the conservative Howard goverment were probably not enough to cut unemployment.
"These changes, simplifying and streamlining arrangements and making it easier to strike (wage) bargains, seem to be a move in the right direction," he said.
"My guess, however, is that this will not complete the process."

In his speech, the central bank chief showed a strong preference for the free market model of the United States rather than the highly regulated labour markets of Europe, where despite high economic growth the jobless rate remains stubbornly high like Australia.
"There is a bigger dimension to Australia's unemployment problem than managing the business cycle," he said.
"A common perception, that if we could only grow faster, unemployment would go away, is missing an important part of the story," he said

Appointed by the government late last year and normally seen as sympathetic to its macro-economic policies, Macfarlane also dampened the hopes of Prime Minister John Howard and Treasurer Peter Costello since the 1997/98 budget was handed down on Tuesday night for lower interest rates.
Recent wages data, he said, had been a setback to prospects for improving inflation.
"If we get good news and our assessment is for lower growth in wages and prices, we can, other things equal, let the econmy run faster," he said.
"This may be done by reducing interest rates or, depending on the cicumstances, refraining from raising them."
"If on the other hand we are getting bad news, we may have to tighten or forego an easing," Macfarlane said.

The RBA has an inflation target of 2-3 percent, which if met constantly can allow for monetary policy reductions to boost economic growth. Rate cuts, however, also depend on wages growth of less than 4.5 percent, a level which is now being challenged by recent pay deals.
Prime Minister John Howard implemented some changes to the industrial relations system last year after winning the March 1996 election.

But since radical industrial policies had helped the conservatives lose an election in 1993, they promised only moderate changes in last year's election campaign and they stuck to those promises when the new system was enacted.

RBA governors have traditionally avoided getting involved in political issues, especially when those issues are the subject of dispute between the government and opposition. The Labor opposition has opposed the government's labour reforms.
Under the new labour relations process, more workers are expected to strike private deals with their employers, rather than rely on industry wide contracts, "awards", set by the industrial courts.
Unions have no right to be involved if no one invites them into the process.
But the system includes extensive safeguards which, critics claim, stifle the ability of employers and employees to strike deals.
-- Melbourne Bureau 61-3 9286 1421
